I.      Introduction

         Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (“Transwestern”) anticipates seeking
authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or
“Commission”) pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”) to construct,
install, own, operate, and maintain the Desert Southwest Expansion Project (“Project”).
The Project includes approximately 526.5 miles of 48-inch diameter mainline pipeline and
approximately 181.5 miles of lateral pipelines, new compressor stations, and other
aboveground facilities located in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The scheduled
in-service date for the Project is June 2029.
         Transwestern is currently in the Commission’s Pre-Filing Review Process for the
Project, which is designed to encourage early stakeholder involvement and to identify and
resolve issues before a certificate application is filed. As part of that process, FERC Staff
solicits comments from stakeholders to determine the environmental issues to be evaluated
in its environmental report. On July 6, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Scoping
Period Requesting Comments on Environmental Issues, establishing a scoping comment
deadline of August 5, 2026.4 On July 21-23, July 28-30, and August 3, the Commission
held in-person and virtual public scoping meetings.5 Under Section 157.21(f)(9) of the
Commission’s regulations,6 Transwestern’s responses to comments submitted in Docket
No. PF26-9-000 during the scoping period are due within 14 days of its close.
        To ensure a comprehensive review of all comments, Transwestern developed
tracking spreadsheets that capture each commenter’s name, the date of submission, and a
summary of the commenter’s substantive points. This review covered all written
comments submitted during the scoping period through the close of business on
August 5, 2026, late-filed comments submitted through the close of business on
August 11, 2026, and the comments reflected in transcripts of the FERC scoping meetings
that occurred on July 21-23, July 28-30, and August 3, 2026. Each comment was reviewed
to determine the subject matter category(ies) to which it pertained and was then organized
by Resource Report, as applicable, and grouped with other similar comments. Legal and
procedural issues are generally addressed in this Appendix A. Appendix B addresses the
remaining comments regarding potential environmental impacts that will be addressed in
forthcoming draft resource reports.

II.     Response to Select Environmental Issues

        Below, Transwestern responds to select issues and arguments raised relating to
FERC’s review of the Project under the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”),
including several that are outside the scope of this proceeding. For the remainder of issues
raised, see Appendix B for information on the issues and where in the forthcoming
Resource Reports the issues will be addressed.

        A.      The Project’s Alternatives Analysis Considers Reasonable Alternatives
                and Is Properly Tailored to Meet the Goals of the Applicant and the
                Needs of the Project Shippers.

        Several commenters raised concerns related to the scope and extent of FERC’s
alternatives analysis. Many commenters stated that FERC should consider non-fossil fuel
alternatives to the Project, such as electrification, renewable or geothermal energy sources,
energy efficiency, or energy storage system alternatives to new natural gas supply.7 Others
request that FERC consider a “geothermal power block” as a non-pipeline alternative for
supplying energy.8 NEPA does not require that FERC analyze these non-gas alternatives
when reviewing a proposal for an interstate natural gas pipeline, and FERC therefore does
not need to expand the scope of its alternatives analysis.

        NEPA requires an agency to consider only reasonable alternatives to its proposed
action; in other words, alternatives that “meet the purpose and need of the proposal” and
that are “technically and economically feasible.”9 Here, the purpose and need for
Transwestern’s proposed project would be the transport of natural gas supply from the
Permian basin in Texas to delivery points in New Mexico and Arizona to meet growing
demand for additional natural gas supplies, driven by the growing need for additional
reliable natural gas-powered electric generation and natural gas deliveries from local
distribution companies with whom Transwestern has executed long-term, binding
precedent agreements. Once Transwestern has applied for a certificate, FERC’s proposed
action would be the issuance of the certificate authorizing the construction and operation
of Transwestern’s new natural gas pipeline and compressor station facilities for that
above-mentioned purpose and need.10 Transwestern considered renewable and non-gas
energy sources, like those commenters raise, in draft Resource Report 10 and concluded
that renewable alternatives do not meet this purpose and need.11 Departing entirely from
the Project’s stated purpose and need would violate NEPA, as courts have long held that

         The comments of Arizona Public Service Company (“APS”) filed during the
scoping period are particularly helpful in addressing this issue.13 NEPA does not require
FERC to consider different energy sources or non-gas alternatives in its NEPA review of
the Project.14 As APS explained, the NGA gives FERC authority over interstate natural
gas facilities, not over the energy generation facilities those facilities supply, and it does

        Some commenters argue that when FERC considers the “no action” alternative, it
must assume that no additional pipeline is constructed and that other renewable projects
may be constructed instead.16 However, NEPA does not require FERC to ignore the
context underlying the need for the Project. Here, the no action alternative reflects the
scenario where a certificate is not issued and the Project is not constructed. Courts do not

unrealistic future events.17 Rather, where a choice of “no action” by an agency would result
in predictable actions by others, the agency must consider those reasonably foreseeable
consequences in its no action alternative.18 And, as Transwestern has explained in draft
Resource Report 10, demand for reliable energy will continue to increase in the Project
area, driven by various factors like population growth and industrial development,
regardless of whether the Project is developed. Thus, the predictable consequence of this
Project not being developed is that other projects would seek to meet that demand using
natural gas delivered by various new pipeline projects.19 As APS explained, “APS’s
decision to contract for natural gas transportation capacity reflects a determination, made

Renewable energy sources do not provide the reliability or the capacity necessary to meet

        Other commenters assert that Transwestern did not adequately consider electric-
power compressor stations.22 To the contrary, Transwestern evaluated the potential to use
electric motor-driven compressors as an alternative to gas-fired compression in draft

not a suitable alternative given extended timelines for required electrical infrastructure,
concerns related to electrical infrastructure reliability, similar or greater environmental
impacts that would result from the need to develop the requisite infrastructure to support
electric compression, and the substantially higher capital and operating costs of such
compressors. NEPA does not require more.

        Several commenters request that additional alternatives, such as various routing and
siting alternatives, be included in FERC’s alternatives analysis. As noted in Appendix B,
an updated routing and siting alternatives analysis will be included in the draft Resource

no causal chain linking the Project with the Project Jupiter data center development.
Moreover, the Project and Project Jupiter lack significant temporal overlap. Project
Jupiter’s initial operations beginning in Q4 2026 and its initial phase will be completed by

Further, Project Jupiter and any other future data centers would be constructed, developed,
and operated by third parties. And finally, FERC lacks authority over the siting or
construction of data centers, including Project Jupiter or any other development. These
factors break any causal chain between the Project and data center development such that
any impacts associated with data centers are not reasonably foreseeable impacts of the
Project. Nevertheless, as a conservative measure, Transwestern has included within the
scope of its analysis of the Project’s potential impacts, the environmental context within
which those impacts may be felt. That context includes, where relevant, impacts from other
projects occurring in the vicinity. Thus, the environmental analysis does not ignore the
potential effect of various Project impacts that overlap geographically and temporally.31

                  2.       FERC Is Not Required to Analyze Upstream Impacts.

         Sierra Club states that if the Commission considers the upstream benefits the
Project will produce, it must also consider upstream environmental impacts, such as GHG
emissions of increased natural gas production48 and impacts to Tribal and cultural resources
from upstream infrastructure development.49 Other commenters, including Sierra Club,
raise various concerns related to impacts associated with fracking and increased production
in the Permian basin,50 including impacts to groundwater,51 water supply,52 and geological
risks.53

        The NGA does not obligate the Commission to assess upstream or downstream
impacts.54 As noted below, the Commission will weigh the Project’s public benefits
against its potential adverse effects in determining whether the Project is required by the
public convenience and necessity, and Transwestern will make that showing in the
application.55

       NEPA does not require FERC to consider upstream emissions or other effects in its
environmental review of the Project. NEPA requires agencies to consider the reasonably
foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed agency action; here, such action is the
approval of the Project.56 But upstream emissions from natural gas production are only
reasonably foreseeable if the agency can reasonably predict both the “number and location
of any additional wells” drilled “as a result of production demand” created by a project.57
